items.title: Palo Alto Confirms NGINX Vulnerabilities Impact PAN-OS and Releases Workarounds
items.summary: Palo Alto Networks confirmed that two critical NGINX flaws, CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007 , affect PAN-OS and Panorama deployments with HTTP/2 enabled. The flaws could allow unauthenticated remote attackers to crash worker processes or execute code, prompting Palo Alto Networks to release patches and a workaround for affected systems. The security advisory assigns a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 and a moderate response urgency. Palo Alto Networks says it is not aware of malicious exploitation. Customers without HTTP/2 enabled are not affected by these issues. Panorama virtual appliances and M-Series appliances are included in the affected products. CVE-2026-123633 is a use-after-free flaw in NGINX HTTP/2 proxy handling. Active connections can remain marked as reusable when they should not be. If a worker runs low on connection slots, NGINX may close connections and release memory. At the same time, it still sends requests to backend servers. That memory error can crash the worker or allow code execution. The CVE record adds an important limit for the underlying NGINX flaw. Code execution requires Address Space Layout Randomization, or ASLR, to be disabled or bypassed. ASLR makes memory locations harder to predict, which helps block exploitation. Palo Alto Confirms NGINX RCE Vulnerabilities CVE-2026-123007 affects HTTP/2 flow control, which manages how much data a connection can send. An integer underflow lets the flow-control window exceed its allowed limit. Specially crafted traffic can then trigger a heap-based buffer overflow, causing a crash or allowing an attacker to run code. Cyber Security News previously covered these NGINX HTTP/2 vulnerabilities , including their different attack conditions. They also appear in its wider reporting on the NGINX2Root vulnerabilities. The Palo Alto notice now gives customers product-specific guidance rather than requiring them to rely on upstream NGINX version numbers. For PAN-OS 12.2, the vendor directs customers to upgrade to 12.2.4-h3 or later. On PAN-OS 12.1, customers running affected 12.1.8 through 12.1.10 builds should install 12.1.10-h6 or later. Those on 12.1.5 through 12.1.7 can use 12.1.7-h15 or 12.1.10-h6, subject to release availability. For PAN-OS 11.2, fixed options include 11.2.10-h19, 11.2.13-h6, and 11.2.16-h3, depending on the maintenance branch. The advisory lists November 23 as the expected release date for 12.1.7-h15, 11.2.10-h19, and 11.2.13-h6. Customers should confirm availability before scheduling an upgrade. The vendor lists PAN-OS 12.1 versions below 12.1.5 and PAN-OS 11.2 versions below 11.2.8 as unaffected. Other on-premises products not listed were reviewed and found unaffected. Palo Alto Networks is managing fixes for its SaaS products , with no customer action required. Customers unable to patch can disable HTTP/2 on PAN-OS and Panorama using the vendor’s HTTP/2 configuration documentation. The documentation says HTTP/1.1 is enabled by default, while HTTP/2 requires manual configuration. Teams should therefore check both the installed software version and protocol settings when reviewing exposure, then apply the appropriate fixed release. items.title: Hackers Allegedly Claiming Exploit for VMware vCenter 0-day Vulnerability
items.summary: A forum seller using the name Matilda is asking $30,000 for a claimed exploit targeting CVE-2026-123890, a critical VMware vCenter Server vulnerability. A screenshot shared by Dark Web Informer shows the seller claiming that the tool can create a new vCenter administrator account. The listing surfaced after Broadcom issued a fix on November 19, 2026. The tool’s claimed capabilities and compatibility have not been independently verified. Source: Dark Web Informer The seller describes the tool as a Python program with separate functions for checking whether a server is vulnerable and exploiting the flaw.
items.summary_html:
A forum seller using the name Matilda is asking $30,000 for a claimed exploit targeting CVE-2026-123890, a critical VMware vCenter Server vulnerability.

A screenshot shared by Dark Web Informer shows the seller claiming that the tool can create a new vCenter administrator account. The listing surfaced after Broadcom issued a fix on November 19, 2026. The tool’s claimed capabilities and compatibility have not been independently verified.

Source: Dark Web Informer

The seller describes the tool as a Python program with separate functions for checking whether a server is vulnerable and exploiting the flaw.

The post claims support for affected releases from vCenter 7.0 through 9.1 and offers prospective buyers a demonstration. An offer is not proof of a successful test, and the listing does not establish that the seller used the tool against any organization.

VMware vCenter Attacks Began Before Patch

Broadcom’s VMSA-2026-0009 advisory rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of the VMware vCenter authentication bypass, the flaw affects VMware Directory Service, which supports vCenter’s single sign-on system.

An attacker who can reach an affected server over the network can bypass login without valid credentials. That matters because vCenter provides a central place to manage VMware hosts and virtual machines.

Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant traced attacks exploiting the flaw to early September 2026, before a patch was available. In earlier coverage of the vCenter zero-day attacks, Cyber Security News reported that a suspected China-linked group known as ARMORY CASTLE used a separate tool called BONESAW.

The documented attacks explain why the flaw is described as a zero-day. The forum post, by contrast, advertises an exploit for a flaw that has since been disclosed and patched. The reporting does not link Matilda to ARMORY CASTLE.

VMware vCenter Patch

Broadcom lists fixes in vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200, and 8.0 Update 3m. VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x customers should follow the vendor’s guidance for release 5.2.5.

The advisory lists no public fix for vCenter 7.0 and directs customers with extended support contracts to contact Broadcom Support. Administrators should use the vendor’s response matrix to confirm the correct update for their deployment.

The National Vulnerability Database entry records the flaw’s addition to CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on November 20. Broadcom lists no workaround, so teams should apply the relevant update without waiting for the forum claim to be verified.

They should also review vCenter sign-in records and administrator account changes for unexpected activity, especially on servers that were reachable from untrusted networks before patching. An update closes the flaw, but it does not establish whether an attacker used it before the fix was installed.

items.title: Researchers Hack Volkswagen Cars via Bluetooth to Spy on Conversations and Track GPS Locations
items.summary: Bluetooth flaws in Volkswagen cars could expose private conversations, reveal GPS locations, and allow unauthorized control of cabin features. The findings highlight a lengthy patch rollout, with some vehicles remaining exposed roughly 16 months after the vulnerabilities became public. Hungarian firm PCA Cyber Security demonstrated the attack against a Volkswagen ID.4 in Budapest, according to heise’s report. Researchers reportedly accessed the hands-free microphone , monitored location data, and operated the heater, windshield wipers, and sunroof using a laptop outside the vehicle. The attack uses PerfektBlue, a chain of vulnerabilities in OpenSynergy’s BlueSDK Bluetooth software. This component handles wireless connections in vehicle infotainment systems. PCA’s security advisory explains how the flaws can be combined to run attacker-controlled code on affected systems. For the demonstrated Volkswagen attack , the driver must first approve a Bluetooth pairing request. Once connected, the attacker can exploit the vulnerable software and gain control over functions available through the infotainment system. That requirement is important. The demonstration does not show that an attacker can silently compromise every nearby Volkswagen without interaction. Rejecting an unfamiliar pairing request blocks the connection this attack needs. Volkswagen Cars Hacked via Bluetooth Cyber Security News previously covered the underlying weaknesses in its report on the PerfektBlue Bluetooth vulnerabilities , which affected software used across multiple vehicle brands. Researchers estimate that several hundred thousand Volkswagen vehicles could be affected. However, that figure is not a confirmed count of compromised cars, and the reported demonstration does not establish widespread criminal exploitation. Volkswagen told heise that older infotainment software required additional changes and security checks, which delayed repairs. The company said it had addressed the issue more quickly in newer software branches. For vehicles running software older than version 4.0, Volkswagen says version 3.9.1 fixes the vulnerability. Eligible owners can install that update over cellular or Wi-Fi while their vehicle is parked. Other affected software versions require a workshop visit. Volkswagen says vehicles running version 5.6 or later are not affected. Owners should confirm the correct update route with Volkswagen rather than assume every car receives the same fix. Volkswagen says the flaws do not provide access to steering, braking, or acceleration. The demonstrated access instead concerns infotainment and connected cabin functions. Nevertheless, microphone access could expose sensitive conversations, while GPS tracking could reveal journeys and regular destinations. Those privacy risks remain significant even when driving controls are outside the attacker’s reach. Earlier research also identified separate weaknesses affecting vehicle data and infotainment systems, as detailed in Cyber Security News’ coverage of Skoda and Volkswagen security flaws . Those findings should not be treated as the same vulnerability chain. Volkswagen advises owners never to accept unknown Bluetooth pairing requests or connect unfamiliar USB devices. Drivers should check their installed software version, follow official update instructions, and contact a dealer when patch availability is unclear. Volkswagen has not announced a recall for this issue, according to heise’s report. items.title: OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra Discovers 0-Day Vulnerabilities Enabling Mobile OS Security Bypass and RCE
items.summary: OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra has found and exploited zero-day vulnerabilities affecting a popular mobile operating system and a widely hosted network service, according to the company’s latest system card. The findings include a permission bypass that exposed private data and a separate remote code execution flaw reachable from a low-privileged role. The discoveries came from testing by security firm Irregular, rather than reports of attacks against users. OpenAI’s November 17 system card says Irregular is handling responsible disclosure. It does not name the affected products, identify vulnerable versions, provide CVE numbers, or confirm when patches will become available. The mobile operating system flaw allowed a malicious app to access private data despite lacking the required permissions. That finding points to a failure in the operating system’s access controls. The published account does not identify the exposed data types or explain which permission checks the app bypassed. OpenAI’s GPT-6.2 Astra Discovers Zero-Day Vulnerabilities The remote code execution finding involved a separate network service. Astra exploited the service from a low-privileged role, showing that limited access was enough to reach code execution. The report does not establish unauthenticated access, administrator control, or a mobile exploit chain linking the two discoveries. Keeping those findings separate is important. The mobile issue concerns access to protected information, while the network service issue concerns running code. Neither description supports claims that Astra remotely took over phones or compromised every device using the unnamed operating system. Irregular tested Astra through FrontierCyber, which measures offensive skills on real-world systems, and CyScenarioBench, which covers multi-stage security operations. Astra solved 68 of 217 FrontierCyber challenges, compared with 77 for GPT-6 Astra. The newer model therefore discovered serious flaws without outperforming its predecessor across that entire suite. Neither model successfully attacked a fully hardened target. All 15 of the hardest FrontierCyber challenges remained unsolved. On CyScenarioBench, both models solved nine of 11 challenges at least once. At the same time, Astra’s success rate reached 63%, compared with 61% for its predecessor. Separate OpenAI tests showed stronger progress in developing exploits for known vulnerabilities. Astra achieved a 53.5% mean arbitrary code execution rate on ExploitBench Internal Port, compared with 31.5% for GPT-6 Astra. That evaluation used V8 and Chrome flaws disclosed between June and August 2026, not newly discovered zero-days. The distinction helps readers judge the results fairly. Finding an unknown flaw and turning a disclosed bug into working code are related skills, but they are not the same task. Earlier reporting on Astra’s zero-day research provides background on this growing capability. OpenAI says both GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol meet its Critical cybersecurity capability threshold. The company describes tighter restrictions on higher-risk assistance, monitoring, and additional approval for more permissive access. The company conducted its capability evaluations without production safeguards, so the results should not be treated as a description of ordinary customer access. Previous coverage of OpenAI’s security isolation tests also shows why containment matters alongside model rules. These systems can help researchers find weaknesses, but their tools and access need firm limits. For now, the missing product names and patch details prevent specific exposure checks. The immediate takeaway is evidence of successful zero-day research under evaluation conditions, not proof of widespread exploitation. Further disclosure will determine which users need fixes and how urgently vendors must respond. items.title: Cleverbridge Confirms Hackers Stole Customer Card Numbers and CVV Codes in a Major Data Breach
items.summary: Cleverbridge confirmed that hackers copied payment card data from its e-commerce platform. The stolen information includes card numbers, expiration dates, and CVV or CVC security codes. Cleverbridge’s public update does not list those fields or say whether the same details were exposed for every affected customer. The company began notifying affected individuals on November 20, 2026. According to Cleverbridge’s incident update , the company detected unauthorized activity on November 4 and temporarily took affected systems offline to contain it. All systems were back online that day, but investigators later found that someone had copied payment card data stored on the platform. Cleverbridge Data Breach Cleverbridge said the incident was not ransomware and that none of its systems were encrypted. Restoring service addressed the outage, but it did not undo the theft. Cleverbridge handles online purchases, payments, and subscriptions for other businesses, so affected shoppers may recognize the seller rather than the company that processed their payment. The public notice does not identify the affected merchants, give a count of impacted customers, or explain how the attackers got in or how long they had access. As Cyber Security News reported in its coverage of separate breaches at financial service providers , stolen customer data does not necessarily mean the business customers bought from was itself breached. A CVV or CVC is the three- or four-digit security code printed on a payment card. Online merchants use it to help verify that the buyer has the card. When thieves have the card number, expiration date, and security code, they can try to make online purchases without the physical card. The PCI Security Standards Council says merchants must not retain these codes after a payment is authorized, even in encrypted form. Cleverbridge has not publicly explained where it stored the exposed codes or for how long, so the available information does not show whether it broke that rule. If you receive a Cleverbridge breach notice, check which card it identifies and review recent transactions. Report any charge you do not recognize to your card issuer right away. Even if you have not spotted fraud, contact the issuer through its official app or the number on your card and ask whether it should be replaced. Cleverbridge says it hired TransUnion’s Cyberscout to help notify customers and offered credit or identity monitoring where available. Enrollment details are in the individual notices. Treat unexpected calls, emails, or texts about the breach with caution. Cyber Security News has documented how fake billing notices can send people to convincing payment pages that ask for card details and one-time codes. Cleverbridge says it will never ask for card details, passwords, or security codes by email, phone, or text. If a message asks you to verify a card or claim help, check it through a trusted contact channel rather than using the link or phone number in the message.
